Near-Zero Downtime: SQL Server (VM) to Azure SQL Database with Transactional Replication

Nithin Sunke · November 1, 2026 · 20 min read

Lab 4 of the Azure SQL Database migration series, and the only method so far where the application keeps running during the migration. The source becomes a publisher, Azure SQL Database a push subscriber, and live banking traffic flows across while we watch. Includes every error hit, from a suspended Agent job to a cleanup that wouldn't clean up.

How transactional replication works

Coming from Oracle, this is the closest thing SQL Server has to one-way GoldenGate:

MSSQLSRV01 (Publisher + Distributor)                          Azure SQL Database
 scsbank ──Log Reader──▶ distribution DB ──Distribution Agent (push)──▶ cisql01/scsbank
          └─Snapshot Agent─▶ B:\ReplData ─────────────────────────────┘  (initial load)
SQL Server replicationOracle GoldenGateRole
Snapshot AgentInitial loadCopies schema and data once
Log Reader AgentExtractReads committed changes from the transaction log
Distribution databaseTrail filesQueues changes
Distribution AgentReplicatApplies changes to the subscriber
Publication / articlesTables in the Extract parameter fileWhat gets replicated

Azure SQL Database can only be a push subscriber. It can't be a publisher or distributor, and the agents can't run inside it. They all run as SQL Server Agent jobs on the VM. Replication is one-way, needs SQL Server 2016 or later, and every replicated table needs a primary key.

Before you start

CheckWhy
Inbound 1433 closed on the VMReplication pushes outbound to Azure, so nothing needs inbound 1433 (see the brute-force finding in Lab 3)
Primary key on every tableAll 17 tables in scsbank have one
Free-tier budgetA continuously running Distribution Agent keeps a serverless database awake, using the free 100,000 vCore seconds in about 1–2 days. Finish the lab and clean up the same day.
In this lab the subscription targets cisql01/scsbank, the database loaded in Lab 3. The articles use @pre_creation_cmd = 'drop', so the snapshot drops and recreates those tables. For a clean run, use a new empty database.

Check prerequisites

1Replication feature installed

A Replication folder in SSMS Object Explorer means the feature is installed. If it's missing, use SQL Server Setup → Add features → SQL Server Replication.

2SQL Server Agent running and automatic

Get-Service SQLSERVERAGENT | Select Name, Status, StartType
Set-Service SQLSERVERAGENT -StartupType Automatic
Start-Service SQLSERVERAGENT

3The real server name

Replication refuses localhost, IP addresses and aliases. Both values must be the actual name:

SELECT @@SERVERNAME AS servername, SERVERPROPERTY('ServerName') AS actual;

4Snapshot folder and Agent account

mkdir B:\ReplData
SELECT servicename, service_account FROM sys.dm_server_services;

Configure the distributor

The VM acts as its own distributor. Run on MSSQLSRV01, connected to master:

EXEC sp_adddistributor @distributor = N'MSSQLSRV01', @password = N'<DistAdminPwd>',
     @trust_distributor_certificate = 'yes';     -- SQL Server 2025, lab only

EXEC sp_adddistributiondb @database = N'distribution', @security_mode = 1;

EXEC sp_adddistpublisher @publisher = N'MSSQLSRV01', @distribution_db = N'distribution',
     @security_mode = 1, @working_directory = N'B:\ReplData';
SQL Server 2025: encryption is strict by default, so a distributor with a self-signed certificate can fail with "certificate chain was issued by an authority that is not trusted". @trust_distributor_certificate = 'yes' is the lab override. In production, install a CA-signed certificate instead.
Warning: The database 'distribution' does not contain database master key. Create database master key and update replication secrets in this database.
Why: replication stores passwords in distribution: the distributor admin password, and later the Azure login. Newer versions want them encrypted with a database master key.
Fix: create the key, then re-save the distributor password so it's stored under the key. Do this before adding the subscription.
USE distribution;
CREATE MASTER KEY ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<StrongDMKPassword>';
GO
USE master;
EXEC sp_changedistributor_password @password = N'<DistAdminPwd>';

SELECT name, is_master_key_encrypted_by_server FROM sys.databases WHERE name = 'distribution';

Create the publication

USE scsbank;
EXEC sp_replicationdboption @dbname = N'scsbank', @optname = N'publish', @value = N'true';
EXEC sp_addlogreader_agent @job_login = NULL, @job_password = NULL, @publisher_security_mode = 1;

EXEC sp_addpublication
     @publication = N'pub_scsbank', @status = N'active', @allow_push = N'true',
     @repl_freq = N'continuous', @independent_agent = N'true',
     @immediate_sync = N'false', @sync_method = N'concurrent';

EXEC sp_addpublication_snapshot @publication = N'pub_scsbank', @publisher_security_mode = 1;

@sync_method = 'concurrent' takes the snapshot without holding table locks for the whole run, so the application keeps working. Then add every table as an article:

DECLARE @s sysname, @t sysname;
DECLARE c CURSOR FOR
  SELECT s.name, t.name FROM sys.tables t JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id
  WHERE t.is_ms_shipped = 0 ORDER BY 1,2;
OPEN c; FETCH NEXT FROM c INTO @s, @t;
WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0
BEGIN
  DECLARE @art sysname = @s + '_' + @t;
  EXEC sp_addarticle
       @publication = N'pub_scsbank', @article = @art,
       @source_owner = @s, @source_object = @t,
       @destination_owner = @s, @destination_table = @t,
       @type = N'logbased',
       @schema_option = 0x00000000080350DF,   -- default + nonclustered indexes (0x40)
       @pre_creation_cmd = N'drop',
       @identityrangemanagementoption = N'manual';
  FETCH NEXT FROM c INTO @s, @t;
END
CLOSE c; DEALLOCATE c;

EXEC sp_addarticle @publication = N'pub_scsbank', @article = N'dbo_GetNums',
     @source_owner = N'dbo', @source_object = N'GetNums', @type = N'func schema only';
The default schema_option doesn't copy nonclustered indexes. Adding 0x40 (giving 0x80350DF) makes the subscriber get them too. Foreign keys are included and marked NOT FOR REPLICATION.

Add the push subscription to Azure

EXEC sp_addsubscription
     @publication = N'pub_scsbank',
     @subscriber = N'cisql01.database.windows.net',
     @destination_db = N'scsbank',
     @subscription_type = N'Push', @sync_type = N'automatic',
     @article = N'all', @update_mode = N'read only',
     @subscriber_type = 0;               -- required for Azure SQL Database
EXEC sp_addpushsubscription_agent
     @publication = N'pub_scsbank',
     @subscriber = N'cisql01.database.windows.net', @subscriber_db = N'scsbank',
     @job_login = NULL, @job_password = NULL,        -- SQL Agent service account
     @subscriber_security_mode = 0,                  -- SQL authentication to Azure
     @subscriber_login = N'nsunke', @subscriber_password = N'<AzurePwd>',
     @frequency_type = 64,                           -- continuous
     @frequency_subday = 4, @frequency_subday_interval = 5;

Snapshot: the initial load

EXEC sp_startpublication_snapshot @publication = N'pub_scsbank';

The first attempt was refused:

Error: SQLServerAgent Error: Request to run job MSSQLSRV01-scsbank-pub_scsbank-1 refused because the job has been suspended.
Why: SQL Server Agent was started before replication was configured, so it hadn't loaded the replication subsystems (Snapshot, LogReader, Distribution). The job had already failed once, and Agent suspended it.

Diagnosis: the subsystems were registered correctly, and the job history showed the earlier failure:

SELECT subsystem, subsystem_dll, agent_exe FROM msdb.dbo.syssubsystems
WHERE subsystem IN ('Snapshot','LogReader','Distribution');
EXEC msdb.dbo.sp_help_job @job_name = N'MSSQLSRV01-scsbank-pub_scsbank-1';

The fix is to restart SQL Server Agent. From a non-elevated PowerShell, that fails too:

Restart Agent from an elevated PowerShell, from SSMS (right-click SQL Server Agent → Restart), or from SQL Server Configuration Manager. After the restart, the snapshot started:

If restarting doesn't help, rebuild the subsystem entries: DELETE FROM msdb.dbo.syssubsystems; EXEC msdb.dbo.sp_verify_subsystems 1;, then restart Agent again. If snapshot.exe, logread.exe or distrib.exe is missing under ...\170\COM\, the Replication feature isn't installed.

Monitoring the initial load

Open Replication Monitor (right-click Replication → Launch Replication Monitor):

Or from T-SQL:

SELECT TOP 20 time, error_text FROM distribution.dbo.MSrepl_errors ORDER BY time DESC;
SELECT TOP 20 time, comments  FROM distribution.dbo.MSdistribution_history ORDER BY time DESC;
The "Unable to complete login process due to delay in login response" error is the same serverless auto-pause we met in Lab 3. The difference: the Distribution Agent retries automatically, so it recovered by itself. BCP just gave up.

Live traffic test

This is what makes replication different from Labs 1–3: the source stays read-write and keeps changing. To prove changes flow, I ran a 5-minute banking workload on the source. Every 2 seconds it ran:

  • A fund transfer between two existing accounts: a debit, a credit and both balance updates in one transaction
  • A card purchase plus a customer login, with every 7th purchase raising a fraud alert
  • Every 10th loop: an EMI repayment, a payee deactivated (update) and an earlier test login deleted
  • Every 25th loop: a 1,000,000 credit that is rolled back, which must never appear on the target

Throughout the test, Replication Monitor stayed at Excellent with near-zero latency. Afterwards, Undistributed Commands was 0: every committed change had been applied to Azure.

Verify on both sides that:

  • Test row counts match.
  • Total account balances are equal.
  • None of the rolled-back credits (IDs 949,xxx,xxx) exist on the target.
-- run on source and target
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Txn.AccountTransaction WHERE TransactionID >= 900000001;
SELECT SUM(Balance) FROM Account.Account;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Txn.AccountTransaction WHERE TransactionID BETWEEN 949000000 AND 949999999;  -- 0

You can also measure end-to-end latency with a tracer token (Replication Monitor → Tracer Tokens → Insert Tracer, or EXEC sp_posttracertoken @publication = N'pub_scsbank').

Cutover

This is the only downtime: usually a few minutes.

  1. Stop the application.
  2. Wait for Undistributed Commands = 0, and for a final tracer token to arrive.
  3. Validate row counts and balances on both sides.
  4. Reseed identity columns on the target. Replicated rows don't advance the identity counter: 
    SELECT 'DBCC CHECKIDENT (''' + s.name + '.' + t.name + ''', RESEED);'
FROM sys.identity_columns ic JOIN sys.tables t ON ic.object_id = t.object_id
JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id;
  5. Remove replication (next section).
  6. Point the application to cisql01.database.windows.net.

Cleanup, and why it failed twice

Don't skip this. While a database is published, its transaction log can't be truncated past what the Log Reader has processed. Leave stopped agents in place and the log grows until the disk fills, just like an Oracle archive-log gap.

Attempt 1: wrong destination name

The script used @destination_db = 'scsbank_repl', but the subscription pointed at scsbank. So sp_dropsubscription failed with "does not exist", and everything after it failed too:

  • The publication couldn't be dropped because a subscription still existed.
  • The still-connected Log Reader blocked sp_replicationdboption.
  • The distributor couldn't be removed.

Attempt 2: publication gone, subscriber still registered

Setting publish to false removes all publications in the database. But the subscriber registration lives in the distributor, so sp_dropdistpublisher still refused.

The working cleanup sequence

-- 0. Check what actually exists first
EXEC sp_helpsubscription @publication = N'pub_scsbank';
EXEC sp_helpsubscriberinfo;

-- 1. Subscription (use the exact destination_db shown above)
USE scsbank;
EXEC sp_dropsubscription @publication = N'pub_scsbank', @article = N'all',
     @subscriber = N'cisql01.database.windows.net', @destination_db = N'scsbank';

-- 2. Publication
EXEC sp_droppublication @publication = N'pub_scsbank';
EXEC sp_replicationdboption @dbname = N'scsbank', @optname = N'publish', @value = N'false';

-- 3. Leftover subscriber registration
USE master;
EXEC sp_dropsubscriber @subscriber = N'cisql01.database.windows.net', @reserved = N'drop_subscriptions';

-- 4. Distributor
EXEC sp_dropdistpublisher @publisher = N'MSSQLSRV01';
EXEC sp_dropdistributiondb @database = N'distribution';
EXEC sp_dropdistributor;
-- last resort: EXEC sp_dropdistributor @no_checks = 1, @ignore_distributor = 1;

-- 5. Verify
EXEC sp_get_distributor;   -- installed = 0
SELECT name, is_published FROM sys.databases WHERE name IN ('scsbank','distribution');

On the Azure side, remove the replication metadata, then delete B:\ReplData on the VM:

EXEC sp_subscription_cleanup @publisher = N'MSSQLSRV01', @publisher_db = N'scsbank',
     @publication = N'pub_scsbank';

All errors and fixes

#ErrorCauseFix
1Distribution database has no master key (warning)Replication secrets should be encrypted with a database master keyCreate the key in distribution, then sp_changedistributor_password
2Job refused because it has been suspended (Msg 22022)Agent started before replication was set up; the job had failed onceRestart SQL Server Agent; if needed, sp_verify_subsystems 1
3Restart-Service: cannot open SQLSERVERAGENT servicePowerShell not running as AdministratorElevated PowerShell, SSMS or Configuration Manager
4Distribution Agent: login timeout / TCP timeout 258Serverless subscriber auto-pausedNone needed: the agent retries automatically
5Subscription does not exist (Msg 14055), then a chain of failuresWrong @destination_db in cleanupCheck sp_helpsubscription first and use exact names
6Only one Log Reader Agent can connect (Msg 18752)Log Reader still running during cleanupDrop the publication first, or wait for the agent to exit
7Cannot drop distribution publisher: Subscribers defined (Msg 21047)Subscriber still registered at the distributorsp_dropsubscriber, or sp_dropdistributor @no_checks = 1

Other issues to watch for

  • "Requires the actual server name": connect SSMS as MSSQLSRV01, not localhost or an IP.
  • Certificate chain not trusted (SQL Server 2025 distributor): run sp_changedistributor_property @property = N'trust_distributor_certificate', @value = N'yes' in a lab; use a CA certificate in production.
  • Snapshot access denied: grant the Agent account (NT Service\SQLSERVERAGENT) Modify permission on the snapshot folder.
  • Indexes missing on the subscriber: add 0x40 to schema_option and reinitialize.
  • Undistributed commands keep growing: check the Distribution Agent history for errors or throttling.

Comparing all four methods

BACPACDMSDACPAC + BCPReplication
DowntimeExport + importWhole migrationExport + import (or deltas)Minutes
Source during migrationFrozenFrozenFrozenFully live
Setup effortLowMediumMediumHigh
Moving partsSqlPackageDMS + SHIRSqlPackage + BCPDistributor + 3 agents + Agent service
Error handlingFails loudlyPortal per tableSilent unless you checkAgents retry; Monitor shows state
Cleanup riskNoneTracking tableData filesLog growth if left behind
Best forSmall, one-offMany DBs, portal visibilityControl, selective reloadsProduction with tight downtime
  • Transactional replication is the only one of these four methods that lets the application keep running during the migration. 149 loops of live banking traffic replicated with the subscriber fully caught up.
  • It has the most moving parts. Agent, subsystems, certificates, master keys and permissions all have to line up.
  • Replication Monitor's Undistributed Commands = 0 is your cutover signal.
  • Plan the cleanup as carefully as the setup. Verify names with sp_helpsubscription, remove things in order, and confirm with sp_get_distributor.
